slides: Open by shifting the mental model from arrows to measurements. A tangent vector is something a covector eats; a covector is a linear measurement attached to a point. The lecture follows the chapter's route through coordinate covectors, differentials, pullbacks, line integrals, and exact versus closed behavior.

Use the hyperplane picture to make a covector visible without smuggling in a metric. In each tangent plane, the kernel line is where omega evaluates to zero, and the parallel unit line is where omega evaluates to one. The check records kernel pairings below 3e-17 and zero unit-line error.

Coordinate covectors transform contravariantly. In polar coordinates, the Jacobian transpose pulls x dy minus y dx back to r squared d theta, and the angular form back to d theta. The numerical pairing error is zero, which is the right invariant to watch.

The differential df is the coordinate-free first derivative of a real-valued function. It is a covector at each point, so its kernel is tangent to the level set. The notebook's residuals shrink with log-log order about 2.12, confirming that df is the first-order part.

Pullbacks reverse direction because covectors compose with pushforwards. A map F pushes tangent vectors forward, so a covector on the target pulls back to the source by testing dF of the source vector. The symbolic chain-rule check gives zero residuals for F star dh equals d of h composed with F.

Line integrals are pullbacks to an interval followed by ordinary integration. In the exact example, straight and curved paths have the same endpoint-controlled value up to tiny numerical error. In the angular example, loops around the missing point integrate to roughly 2*pi, so closed does not mean exact globally.

Use the classifier table to separate three ideas students often blur. Exact fields are conservative and closed; the angular form is closed on the punctured plane but not exact because its loop integral is nonzero; y dx is not closed and therefore cannot be exact.

The cotangent bundle is the dual vector bundle to the tangent bundle, and metrics add an extra bridge. Chapter 10 supplies dual transition functions that preserve pairings; Chapter 13 supplies flat and sharp maps once a Riemannian metric is chosen. Without a metric, df is naturally a covector, not an arrow.

The winding lab turns the angular obstruction into a knob. A path with winding k has integral 2*pi*k, so winding negative two gives about -12.5664, winding zero gives zero, and winding two gives about 12.5664. The integer, not the local formula, detects the global obstruction.

Close by tying the chapter's tools to later differential forms. Covectors are degree-one forms, pullback is contravariant, df is the natural derivative, line integrals test exactness, and the angular form foreshadows de Rham cohomology by showing a closed local object with a global period.
